appraisal_events.evidence: his same faults as Cottard's, 'timidité, désir de plaire, efforts infructueux pour y réussir', had only worsened; his hurried, jargon-filled stories only 'sembler interminable'; 'personne n'allait jusqu'à assumer la responsabilité, à risquer l'adhésion publique d'un éclat de rire', leaving Saniette 'désolé' and smiling alone to himself; later, alarmed by Cottard's expulsion of a peasant, he 'feignit d'avoir mal au ventre' so as not to be associated with the scene.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator repeatedly frames Saniette as the clan's chronic, quietly tolerated failure: his attempts at wit misfire, no one will risk openly supporting him, and he later cravenly hides during Cottard's aggressive scene, confirming his marginal and faintly pathetic standing among the fidèles.

appraisal_events.evidence: her unbroken fidelity made her 'plus qu'une «fidèle» ordinaire, la fidèle type, l'idéal que Mme Verdurin avait longtemps cru inaccessible... incarné en cette nouvelle recrue féminine'; yet she is 'Brouillée avec sa famille, exilée de son pays', living in a pension and following the Verdurins on their travels, so wholly absorbed that the narrator closes by citing Vigny's line on the one true beloved, 'Toi seule me parus ce qu'on cherche toujours', applied to her attachment to Mme Verdurin.
appraisal_events.explanation: Sherbatoff is elevated to the status of Mme Verdurin's ideal, model fidèle, but this elevation is explicitly grounded in her estrangement from her own family and exile from wider society, and the closing literary citation applies a line about true love to a substitute devotion with evident irony.

status_effects.explanation: Saniette is repeatedly shown as socially inept, unable to land a story or earn even minimal public backing from the group.
His position among the fidèles remains marginal and mildly pitiable despite his long tenure in the clan.
She achieves total, unrivaled inclusion in the little clan, becoming Mme Verdurin's ideal, ever-present companion and, in her own words, 'family'.
This total absorption into the clan is presented as bound up with her estrangement from her own family and exile from wider society, a real diminishment beneath the local elevation.

ambiguities: The elevation of princesse Sherbatoff as Mme Verdurin's 'ideal fidèle' is entangled with her isolation from family and society, and the closing citation from Vigny is applied with apparent literary irony, so it is uncertain whether the passage endorses this outcome as good fortune or frames it as a poignant substitute for real intimacy.
